## Abstract

Catastrophic forgetting remains a primary obstacle for continual learning in neural networks. This work investigates whether the modularity of Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) is an effective inductive bias against it in class-incremental learning. Comparing an SMoE with a dense multilayer perceptron on MNIST, a benchmark of handwritten digits, including a three-task extension, and on CIFAR-10, we find that modularity alone offers no retention advantage. Freezing experts trades plasticity for retention, and its plasticity cost arises from earlier classes winning the final decision rather than from a failure to learn the new task. The router does specialize experts around visual primitives, but the shared projection feeding it keeps moving the latent space; with three tasks, this drift erases the earliest task while recency bias overtakes the intermediate one. Removing the projection at equal parameter count raises retention by about 30 points, at a cost in plasticity. With the projection, only an oracle router surpasses the dense baseline without sacrificing plasticity, pointing to learned routing as the main bottleneck. Code is available at [https://github.com/tucozz/smoe_incremental_learning](https://github.com/tucozz/smoe_incremental_learning).
